"The Darwin night hummed with cicadas and the distant pulse of the airport. Inside the caged rear compartment of the police van, the world shrank to cold steel, the smell of stale sweat, and the echo of his own ragged breath. Dale Scott Walkinshaw, twenty-three, pressed his forehead against the mesh divider. Through the grille, he saw the flashing lights painting the palm trees red and blue—the very trees he’d wrapped his Hilux around hours earlier. He’d held her so carefully, that young woman from the bar, her head lolling against his shoulder as she drifted in and out of consciousness. *Her back*, he’d begged the officers. *Please, check her back.* But the breathalyzer’s verdict—0.149—had sealed his fate. Now, alone in the rolling cage, guilt curdled into something sharper. The alcohol haze lifted, leaving raw terror: *What if she doesn’t walk again? What if it’s my fault?*

Outside, Senior Constable Evans radioed dispatch, his voice tight with routine. 'Subject secured. Awaiting transport to cells.' He glanced at the van’s solid rear doors. No camera lens peered back. No internal monitor glowed on his dashboard. Just silence. He remembered the briefing months ago—a memo about 'enhanced welfare checks' after that incident in Alice Springs. He’d filed it away. Everyone had. What was one more drunk kid in the back? He checked his watch. *Twenty minutes since last visual.* Protocol said thirty. He’d look again soon.

But inside, time fractured. Dale’s fingers traced a hairline crack in the welded bench where rust bled like a tear. Sixteen times before him, others had sat right here. Sixteen times, hands had sought escape in teeth, nails, or sharp edges. Six times, officers had opened these doors to find slack jaws and slowing hearts. Dale didn’t know their names. He only knew the crushing weight of the cage—the same cage the 2013 report had screamed to fix. His vision tunneled. The palm fronds outside blurred into the bars of his childhood bedroom window, then his father’s disappointed eyes. A sob caught in his throat. *It wasn’t a matter of if*, the coroner would later write, *but when.*

He didn’t see Constable Lee approach the van forty minutes later, coffee in hand, humming along to the radio. He didn’t hear the key scrape the lock. He only knew the sudden, shocking cold of the metal against his wrist as he slumped forward—a final, silent protest against the indifference of steel and silence.

The door swung open. 'Walkinshaw? Hey—' Lee’s coffee hit the asphalt. Evans sprinted over, shouting for backup, for an ambulance, for anything. But the van held only stillness. Only the ghost of a young man who’d been deemed 'just another drunk' until it was too late.

Months later, Coroner Greg Cavanagh’s words would hang over the Territory like monsoon humidity: *Failed to act. Ignored warnings. Sixteen attempts.* Dale’s name would join the ledger—not as a statistic, but as the boy who loved palm trees until he crashed into one, who held a stranger with tenderness, and who died unseen in a cage the system refused to see. Outside the courtroom, a single frangipani petal drifted onto the Stuart Highway, unnoticed."

Outside, Senior Constable Evans radioed dispatch, his voice tight with routine. 'Subject secured. Awaiting transport to cells.' He glanced at the van’s solid rear doors. No camera lens peered back. No internal monitor glowed on his dashboard. Just silence. He remembered the briefing months ago—a memo about 'enhanced welfare checks' after that incident in Alice Springs. He’d filed it away. Everyone had. What was one more drunk kid in the back? He checked his watch. *Twenty minutes since last visual.* Protocol said thirty. He’d look again soon.

But inside, time fractured. Dale’s fingers traced a hairline crack in the welded bench where rust bled like a tear. Sixteen times before him, others had sat right here. Sixteen times, hands had sought escape in teeth, nails, or sharp edges. Six times, officers had opened these doors to find slack jaws and slowing hearts. Dale didn’t know their names. He only knew the crushing weight of the cage—the same cage the 2013 report had screamed to fix. His vision tunneled. The palm fronds outside blurred into the bars of his childhood bedroom window, then his father’s disappointed eyes. A sob caught in his throat. *It wasn’t a matter of if*, the coroner would later write, *but when.*

He didn’t see Constable Lee approach the van forty minutes later, coffee in hand, humming along to the radio. He didn’t hear the key scrape the lock. He only knew the sudden, shocking cold of the metal against his wrist as he slumped forward—a final, silent protest against the indifference of steel and silence.

The door swung open. 'Walkinshaw? Hey—' Lee’s coffee hit the asphalt. Evans sprinted over, shouting for backup, for an ambulance, for anything. But the van held only stillness. Only the ghost of a young man who’d been deemed 'just another drunk' until it was too late.

Months later, Coroner Greg Cavanagh’s words would hang over the Territory like monsoon humidity: *Failed to act. Ignored warnings. Sixteen attempts.* Dale’s name would join the ledger—not as a statistic, but as the boy who loved palm trees until he crashed into one, who held a stranger with tenderness, and who died unseen in a cage the system refused to see. Outside the courtroom, a single frangipani petal drifted onto the Stuart Highway, unnoticed."
